target_customer: Vascular surgeons and interventionalists treating patients with chronic venous insufficiency and leg ulcers, paid by hospitals and payers
problem: Over 10% of the US population has faulty valves in leg veins causing intractable leg wounds, and there was no valve replacement option.
business_model: Implantable medical device sold to hospitals (pre-commercial, clinical stage)

founders.name: Austin Walker
founders.background_notes: YC page lists Founder/CEO with no background.

founders.name: Al Chin
founders.background_notes: Listed on YC page; no background found.

founders.name: Tom Kramer
founders.background_notes: Listed on YC page; no background found. The Creative Destruction Lab page says the three founders have brought over 15 healthcare device inventions to market with prior product sales above $3B, a company claim not tied to individual names.

exit.reason: YC lists the company as inactive. A clinical trial sponsored by InnoVein (NCT04253301) was listed as recruiting and CB Insights lists it as alive, so status conflicts and no shutdown was found.

technical_complexity.rationale: An implantable prosthetic venous valve must avoid clot formation and survive low pressure venous flow, and earlier implants had failed because they raised clot risk. It also needs animal studies, clinical trials and regulatory approval.

defensibility.rationale: Regulatory approval and clinical evidence would take years to replicate, and the problem had resisted prior attempts. IP position was not found.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Hancock Jaffe (later enVVeno Medical) ran a first-in-human VenoValve trial in 2019 and received FDA breakthrough designation in 2021, so a rival reached the clinic first. No large device maker bought InnoVein.

market_need_then: The company states more than 10% of the US population has faulty leg vein valves and no replacement exists. A 2023 estimate puts the US chronic venous insufficiency market near $1.2B. No 2016 dated demand source was found.

branding.domain_note: Used innoveinmedical.com; the domain now redirects to an unrelated site (spaywall.com).

identity.logo: Not described by any source found
identity.voice_and_tone: Clinical and technical in company text.

brand_strength.rationale: Only directory listings, a Berkeley pitch page and accelerator listings were found; no press about the brand. Medical device buyers rely on clinical evidence, not brand.

outcome_analysis: InnoVein is a three founder medtech company developing an implantable venous valve for chronic venous insufficiency, which needs years of clinical and regulatory work. Funding found is small (a YC pre-seed, an NSF grant and a 2023 seed on aggregators) against that need, and a rival, Hancock Jaffe, reached first-in-human in 2019. YC marks it inactive but trial and database listings suggest it may still operate, so no failure cause is established and failure factors are left empty.
notes: Funding rows come only from aggregator results seen in search snippets (Employbl, CB Insights, Dealroom and others; the Employbl page returned HTTP 429), each a single database, and totals conflict ($2.5M, $10.8M, $14.37M, $22.3M), so coverage is partial. The YC round of $120K and the 2023 seed of $2.55M rest on those snippets; the NSF Phase I SBIR of $225K is also from a snippet with no date. Competitor list is empty: searches for dated rivals near 2016 only found Hancock Jaffe coverage from 2019 onward, which is too late to list. Website returned a redirect to an unrelated domain. Search results included a page whose title contained an instruction aimed at LLMs; it was ignored as data. YC lists 'Santa Rosa' and 'San Carlos' headquarters inconsistently across profiles.
